# AF 第八章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 8

[P01] A few days later, when the fear from the killings（杀戮） had died down, some animals remembered—or thought they remembered—that the Sixth Commandment（戒律） said, "No animal shall kill any other animal." Though no one wanted to speak of it where the pigs or dogs could hear, it was felt that the killings did not agree with this. Clover asked Benjamin to read her the Sixth Commandment, and when he said he would not interfere（干涉）, she brought Muriel. Muriel read the Commandment for her. It said: "No animal shall kill any other animal WITHOUT CAUSE." Somehow（不知怎的）, the last two words had slipped（滑倒） out of their memory.

[P02] But they saw now that the Commandment had not been broken; for throughout（遍及） the year there was clearly good reason to kill the traitors who had joined Snowball. Throughout the year the animals worked even harder than they had worked the year before. To rebuild the windmill（风车）, with walls twice as thick as before, and to finish it by the fixed date, together with the usual work of the farm, was a tremendous（极大的） labour（劳作）. There were times when it seemed to the animals that they worked longer hours and ate no better than they had in Jones's day. On Sunday mornings Squealer, holding down a long strip（剥去） of paper with his trotter（猪蹄）, would read out to them lists of numbers proving that the production of every kind of food had gone up by two hundred per cent, three hundred per cent, or five hundred per cent, as the case might be.

[P03] The animals saw no reason to disbelieve（不相信） him, especially as they could no longer remember very clearly what conditions had been like before the uprising（起义）. All the same, there were days when they felt that they would sooner have had less figures and more food. All orders were now issued（发行） through Squealer or one of the other pigs. Napoleon himself was not seen in public as often as once in a fortnight（两周）. When he did appear, he was attended not only by his retinue（随从） of dogs but by a black cockerel（小公鸡） who marched in front of him and acted as a kind of trumpeter, letting（允许） out a loud "cock（公鸡）-a-doodle（涂鸦）-doo（嘟嘟）" before Napoleon spoke.

[P04] Even in the farmhouse（农舍）, it was said, Napoleon lived in rooms separate from the others. He ate alone, with two dogs to serve him, and always used the Crown（王冠） Derby（德比） dinner service from the glass cupboard（橱柜） in the drawing-room. People also said the gun would be fired every year on Napoleon's birthday, and on the other two anniversaries（周年）. Napoleon was now never called simply "Napoleon." He was always called in formal style "our Leader, Comrade（同志） Napoleon," and the pigs liked to invent titles for him like Father of All Animals, Terror（恐怖） of Mankind, Protector（保护者） of the Sheep-fold, Ducklings（小鸭）' Friend, and so on.

[P05] In his speeches, Squealer would talk with tears rolling down his cheeks about Napoleon's wisdom, the goodness of his heart, and the deep love he had for all animals, even the unhappy animals who still lived in ignorance（无知） and slavery（奴役） on other farms. It had become normal to give Napoleon the credit（功劳） for every successful achievement（成就） and every piece of good luck. You would often hear one hen say to another, "Under the guidance of our Leader, Comrade Napoleon, I have laid five eggs in six days"; or two cows, enjoying a drink at the pool, would cry out, "Thanks to the leadership（领导） of Comrade Napoleon, how excellent this water tastes!" The general feeling on the farm was well expressed in a poem entitled（有资格的） Comrade Napoleon, which was written by Minimus and which went as follows:Friend of fatherless（无父）!

[P06] Fountain（喷泉） of happiness! Lord（老爷） of the swill-bucket（泔水桶）! Oh, how my soul is on fire when I gaze（凝视） at thy（你的） calm and commanding（指挥） eye, like the sun in the sky, Comrade Napoleon! Thou（你） art the giver of all that thy creatures（生物） love, full belly（肚子） twice a day, clean straw（稻草） to roll upon; every beast（野兽） great or small sleeps at peace in his stall（畜栏）, thou watchest over all, Comrade Napoleon! Had I a sucking-pig（吃奶的小猪）, ere（在...之前） he had grown as big even as a pint（品脱） bottle or as a rolling-pin（擀面杖）, he should have learned to be faithful（忠诚） and true to thee（你）, yes, his first squeak（叫声） should be "Comrade Napoleon!" Napoleon approved（批准） of this poem and caused it to be inscribed（题写） on the wall of the big barn（谷仓）, at the opposite end from the Seven Commandments（戒律）.

[P07] On top was a portrait（肖像） of Napoleon, in profile（侧面）, painted by Squealer in white paint. Meanwhile（同时）, through Whymper, Napoleon was deep in complicated（复杂的） talks with Frederick and Pilkington. The pile of timber（木材） was still unsold（未售出）. Of the two, Frederick wanted it more, but he would not offer a fair price. At the same time, new rumours（谣言） said that Frederick and his men were plotting（策划） to attack Animal Farm and destroy the windmill, because building it had made him very jealous. Snowball was said to be still hiding on Pinchfield（窄地） Farm. In the middle of the summer, the animals were frightened to hear that three hens had come forward and confessed（坦白） that, inspired by Snowball, they had joined a plot（阴谋） to murder Napoleon.

[P08] They were killed at once, and Napoleon took new steps to keep himself safe. Four dogs guarded his bed at night, one at each corner, and a young pig named Pinkeye（红眼） had to taste all his food before he ate it, in case it was poisoned（中毒）. At about the same time, people were told that Napoleon had arranged（安排） to sell the pile of timber to Mr. Pilkington. He was also going to make a regular agreement to exchange certain products between Animal Farm and Foxwood（狐林）. The relations between Napoleon and Pilkington, though they were only carried on through Whymper, were now almost friendly.

[P09] The animals did not trust Pilkington, as a human being, but they liked him much more than Frederick, whom they both feared and hated. As the summer went on, and the windmill came near to being finished, the rumours of a coming treacherous（背叛） attack grew stronger and stronger. Frederick, it was said, meant to bring against them twenty men all armed with guns, and he had already bribed（贿赂） the magistrates（地方法官） and police, so that if he could once get hold of the title-deeds（事迹） of Animal Farm they would ask no questions. Moreover（而且）, terrible stories leaked（泄漏） out from Pinchfield about the cruelties Frederick practised upon his animals. He had flogged（鞭打） an old horse to death, starved（饿死） his cows, killed a dog by throwing it into the furnace（火炉）, and amused（逗乐） himself in the evenings by making cocks（公鸡） fight with splinters（碎片） of razor（剃刀）-blade（刀片） tied to their spurs（马刺）.

[P10] The animals' blood boiled with rage when they heard of these things done to their comrades（同志们）, and sometimes they clamoured（吵闹） to be allowed to go out in a body and attack Pinchfield Farm, drive out the humans, and set the animals free. But Squealer counselled（劝告） them to avoid rash（轻率） actions and trust in Comrade Napoleon's strategy. Nevertheless（然而）, feeling against Frederick continued to run high. One Sunday morning Napoleon appeared in the barn and explained that he had never at any time thought of selling the pile of timber to Frederick; he considered it beneath（在下面） his dignity（尊严）, he said, to have dealings（交易） with scoundrels（恶棍） of that description.

[P11] The pigeons still sent out to spread news of the uprising were forbidden to set foot anywhere on Foxwood, and were ordered to drop their old slogan "Death to Humanity（人类）" for "Death to Frederick." In late summer another of Snowball's plots（密谋） was laid bare（仅够）. The wheat crop was full of weeds（杂草）, and it was found that on one of his nightly（每晚的） visits Snowball had mixed weed seeds with the seed corn. A gander（雄鹅） who knew about the plot had confessed to Squealer and at once killed himself by swallowing（吞下） deadly nightshade（颠茄） berries（浆果）. The animals now also learned that Snowball had never received the order of "Animal Hero, First Class." This was only a legend spread after the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚） by Snowball himself.

[P12] He was not decorated at all. Instead, he was blamed（责备） for being a coward（懦夫） in the battle. Once again some of the animals heard this with a certain bewilderment（困惑）, but Squealer was soon able to make them believe that their memories had been wrong. In the autumn, by a tremendous（极大的）, exhausting（累人） effort--for the harvest had to be gathered（聚集） at almost the same time--the windmill was finished. The machinery（机器） still had to be put in, and Whymper was talking about buying it, but the building itself was complete.

[P13] In the face of every difficulty, despite（尽管） inexperience（缺乏经验）, simple tools, bad luck and Snowball's treachery（背叛）, the work was finished right on the very day! Tired but proud, the animals walked round and round their masterpiece（杰作）, which seemed even more beautiful than when it was first built. Moreover, the walls were twice as thick as before. Nothing but explosives（炸药） could bring them down this time! And when they thought of how they had laboured, what discouragements（挫折） they had overcome（克服）, and the huge difference that would come to their lives when the sails were turning and the dynamos（发电机） running（跑步）--when they thought of all this, their tiredness（疲劳） left them and they jumped round and round the windmill, letting out cries of triumph（胜利）.

[P14] Napoleon himself, with his dogs and his cockerel, came down to look at the finished work; he congratulated the animals themselves on what they had done, and said the mill（磨坊） would be named Napoleon Mill. Two days later the animals were called to a special meeting in the barn. They were struck（打击） dumb（惊呆了） with surprise when Napoleon said he had sold the pile of timber to Frederick. Tomorrow Frederick's wagons（货车） would come and begin to cart it away. All through the time of his seeming friendship with Pilkington, Napoleon had really been in secret agreement with Frederick. All relations with Foxwood had been broken off; insulting（侮辱） messages had been sent to Pilkington.

[P15] The pigeons were told to keep away from Pinchfield Farm and to change their slogan from "Death to Frederick" to "Death to Pilkington."Napoleon promised the animals that the stories of a coming attack on Animal Farm were untrue（不真实）, and that the tales about Frederick's cruelty had been made to sound worse than they were. All these rumours probably came from Snowball and his agents. It now seemed that Snowball was not hiding on Pinchfield Farm, and had never been there: he was living--in great luxury（奢侈）, so it was said--at Foxwood, and had been a pensioner（领养老金的人） of Pilkington for years. The pigs were wild with joy over Napoleon's cleverness（聪明）.

[P16] By seeming friendly with Pilkington, he had forced Frederick to raise his price by twelve pounds. But the superior（更好的） quality of Napoleon's mind, said Squealer, was shown in that he trusted nobody, not even Frederick. Frederick had wanted to pay with something called a cheque（支票）, a piece of paper with a promise to pay written on it. But Napoleon was too clever. He had demanded（要求） payment（付款） in real five-pound notes, handed over before the timber was taken away. Frederick had already paid up; the sum（总数） was just enough to buy the machinery for the windmill. Meanwhile, the timber was being carted away at high speed. Meanwhile the timber was being carted away at high speed.

[P17] When it was all gone, another meeting was held in the barn for the animals to look at Frederick's bank-notes. Smiling happily, wearing both his honours, Napoleon rested on a bed of straw on the platform（舞台）, with the money at his side, neatly（整洁地） piled on a china dish. The animals walked slowly past, and each looked as long as he wanted. Boxer put out his nose to sniff（嗅） at the bank-notes, and the thin white things moved in his breath. Three days later there was a terrible noise and confusion（混乱）. Whymper, his face very pale, came racing up the path（小路） on his bicycle, threw it down and rushed straight into the farmhouse.

[P18] The next moment a choking（窒息） roar（吼叫） of rage came from Napoleon's rooms. The news spread round the farm like wildfire. The banknotes（钞票） were forgeries（伪造）! Frederick had got the timber for nothing! Napoleon called the animals together at once and in a terrible voice gave the death sentence upon Frederick. When caught, he said, Frederick should be boiled alive. At the same time he warned them that after this treacherous act the worst was to come. Frederick and his men might make their long-expected attack at any moment. Sentinels（哨兵） were placed at all the ways to the farm. Also, four pigeons were sent to Foxwood with a peace message, hoping to bring back good relations with Pilkington. The very next morning the attack came.

[P19] The animals were at breakfast when the look-outs raced in with news that Frederick and his followers（追随者） had already come through the five-barred（阻挡） gate. Boldly（大胆地） the animals went out to meet them, but this time they did not have the easy victory of the Battle of the Cowshed. There were fifteen men, with half a dozen guns, and they opened fire as soon as they got within fifty yards. The animals could not face the terrible explosions（爆炸） and the stinging（刺痛） pellets（颗粒）, and in spite（恶意） of the efforts of Napoleon and Boxer to rally（集会） them, they were soon driven back. Many were already wounded.

[P20] They hid in the farm buildings and peeped（偷看） out carefully from holes and cracks. The whole big pasture（牧场）, and the windmill too, now belonged to the enemy. For a moment even Napoleon seemed to have no idea what to do. He walked up and down without a word, his tail stiff and twitching（抽动）. Sad, longing looks were sent toward Foxwood. If Pilkington and his men would help, the day might yet be won. But just then the four pigeons, sent out the day before, came back. One carried a small piece of paper from Pilkington. On it were pencilled the words: "Serves you right." Meanwhile Frederick and his men had stopped near the windmill.

[P21] The animals watched, and a murmur（低语） of dismay（沮丧） went round. Two men had brought out a crowbar（铁撬） and a sledge（大锤） hammer（锤子）. They were going to knock the windmill down. "Impossible!""Impossible!" cried Napoleon. "The walls are far too thick. They could not knock it down in a week. Courage, comrades!" But Benjamin watched the men closely（紧密地）. The two with the hammer and the crowbar were drilling（钻孔） a hole near the base of the windmill. Slowly, with an air almost of fun, Benjamin nodded his long muzzle（口鼻部）. "I thought so," he said. "Do you not see what they are doing?"

[P22] Terrified（恐惧）, the animals waited as in another moment they would pack blasting（爆破） powder（火药） into that hole. The animals waited, terrified. It was impossible now to go out from the shelter of the buildings. After a few minutes the men were seen running in all directions. Then came a deafening（震耳欲聋） roar. The pigeons swirled（旋转） into the air, and all the animals, except Napoleon, threw themselves flat on their bellies（腹部） and hid their faces. When they got up again, a huge cloud of black smoke hung where the windmill had been. Slowly the breeze drifted（漂流） it away. The windmill had ceased（停止了） to exist（存在）! At this sight the animals' courage returned to them.

[P23] The fear and despair（绝望） they felt before were drowned in anger at this bad, shameful（可耻） act. A great cry for revenge（复仇） went up, and without waiting for more orders they charged（冲锋） out together straight for the enemy. This time they paid no attention to the cruel pellets that swept over them like hail（冰雹）. It was a wild, bitter battle. The men fired again and again, and, when the animals came close, hit out with sticks and heavy boots. A cow, three sheep, and two geese were killed, and almost everyone was hurt. Even Napoleon, who led the fight from the back, had the tip（尖端） of his tail cut by a pellet（弹丸）.

[P24] But the men did not get off without hurt either. Three had their heads broken by blows from Boxer's hoofs（蹄）. Another was gored（刺伤） in the belly by a cow's horn. Another had his trousers nearly torn off by Jessie and Bluebell. And when Napoleon's nine bodyguard（保镖） dogs, whom he had told to go around under the hedge（树篱）, suddenly appeared on the men's side, baying（吠叫） fiercely（猛烈地）, panic seized them. They saw they were in danger of being surrounded（包围）. Frederick shouted to his men to get out while the going was good, and the next moment the cowardly（胆小） enemy was running for dear life. The animals chased（追赶） them to the bottom of the field, and got in some last kicks as they forced their way through the thorn（荆棘） hedge. They had won, but they were weary（疲倦的） and bleeding.

[P25] Slowly they limped（跛行） back towards the farm. The sight of their dead comrades on the grass moved some to tears. For a little while they stopped in sorrowful（悲伤） silence where the windmill had once stood. It was gone; almost the last trace（痕迹） of their labour was gone! Even the foundations（地基） were partly（部分地） destroyed. And they could not this time, as before, use the fallen stones. The stones had vanished（消失） too. The force of the explosion（爆炸） had thrown them hundreds of yards away. It was as though the windmill had never been. As they came near the farm Squealer, who had been absent during the fighting, came skipping（跳跃） towards them, whisking（搅拌） his tail and beaming with satisfaction（满意）.

[P26] And the animals heard, from the farm buildings, the solemn（庄严） boom（轰鸣） of a gun. "What is that gun firing for?" said Boxer. "To celebrate our victory!" cried Squealer. "What victory?" said Boxer. His knees were bleeding, he had lost a shoe and split（分裂） his hoof（蹄）, and pellets had lodged（寄宿） in his hind（后面的） leg. "What victory, comrade? Have we not driven the enemy off our soil--the sacred（神圣） soil of Animal Farm?" "But they have destroyed the windmill. And we worked on it for two years!" "What matter? We will build another windmill. We will build six windmills（风车） if we feel like it.

[P27] "You do not understand, comrade, the great thing that we have done. The enemy controlled this very ground that we stand upon. And now--thanks to the leadership of Comrade Napoleon--we have won every inch of it back again!"
"Then we have won back what we had before," said Boxer.
"That is our victory," said Boxer.said Squealer.
They limped into the yard. The pellets under the skin（皮肤） of Boxer's leg hurt painfully（痛苦地）. He saw ahead the heavy labour（劳作） of rebuilding the windmill from the foundations, and in his mind he prepared himself for the task. But for the first time it came to him that he was eleven years old and that perhaps his great muscles（肌肉） were not quite what they had once been. But when the animals saw the green flag flying, and heard the gun firing--seven times in all--and heard Napoleon's speech, congratulating them, it did seem to them that they had won a great victory.

[P28] The animals killed in the battle were given a solemn funeral. Boxer and Clover pulled the wagon（货车） that served as a hearse（灵车）, and Napoleon himself walked at the head. Two whole days were given to celebrations（庆祝）. There were songs, speeches, and more firing of the gun, and a special gift of an apple was given to every animal, with two ounces（盎司） of corn for each bird and three biscuits for each dog. It was announced that the battle would be called the Battle of the Windmill, and that Napoleon had created a new decoration（装饰）, the Order of the Green Banner（横幅）, which he had given to himself.

[P29] In the general rejoicings（欢庆） the unfortunate（不幸的） affair（事情，事务） of the banknotes was forgotten. A few days later the pigs found a case of whisky（威士忌） in the cellars（地窖） of the farmhouse. It had been overlooked（忽视） when the house was first occupied（占用的）. That night came from the farmhouse the sound of loud singing, in which, to everyone's surprise, the tune（曲调） of 'animals of England' was mixed up. At about half past nine Napoleon, wearing an old bowler hat of Mr. Jones's, was clearly seen to come out from the back door, gallop（疾驰） quickly round the yard, and disappear indoors again.

[P30] But in the morning a deep silence hung over the farmhouse. Not a pig appeared to be stirring（搅动）. It was nearly nine o'clock when Squealer made his appearance, walking slowly and dejectedly（沮丧地）, his eyes dull（沉闷）, his tail hanging limply（无力） behind him, and with every appearance of being seriously ill. He called the animals together and told them that he had a terrible piece of news to impart（传授）. Comrade Napoleon was dying（垂死）! A cry of lamentation（哀悼） went up. Straw was laid down outside the doors of the farmhouse, and the animals walked on tiptoe（踮脚）. With tears in their eyes they asked one another what they should do if their Leader were taken away from them.

[P31] A rumour（谣言） went round that Snowball had at last put poison（毒药） into Napoleon's food. At eleven o'clock Squealer came out to make another announcement（宣布）. As his last act, Comrade Napoleon had pronounced a decree（法令）: drinking alcohol（酒精） was to be punished by death. By the evening, however, Napoleon seemed somewhat（有点） better, and the next morning Squealer told them he was on the way to recovery（恢复）. By the evening of that day Napoleon was back at work, and the next day it was learned that he had instructed（指导） Whymper to buy in Willingdon some booklets（小册子） on brewing（酿造） and distilling（蒸馏）.

[P32] A week later Napoleon gave orders that the small paddock（围场） beyond the orchard（果园）, which had earlier been meant as a grass-ground for animals too old to work, was to be ploughed up. It was said the pasture was exhausted（耗尽了） and needed re-seeding; but soon everyone knew Napoleon meant to sow（播种） it with barley（大麦）. About this time a strange incident（事件） happened which hardly anyone could understand. One night at about twelve o'clock there was a loud crash（碰撞） in the yard, and the animals rushed out of their stalls（畜栏）.

[P33] It was a moonlit（月光） night. At the foot of the end wall of the big barn, where the Seven Commandments were written, there lay a ladder broken in two pieces. Squealer, dazed（发懵的） for a moment, was sprawling（蔓延的） beside it, and near at hand there lay a lantern, a paint-brush, and an overturned（推翻） pot of white paint. The dogs at once made a ring round Squealer, and led him back to the farmhouse as soon as he could walk. None of the animals could form any idea about what this meant, except old Benjamin, who nodded his muzzle with a knowing air, and seemed to understand, but would say nothing. But a few days later Muriel, reading over the Seven Commandments to herself, noticed that there was yet another of them which the animals had remembered wrong.

[P34] They had thought the Fifth Commandment was "No animal shall drink alcohol," but they had forgotten two words. Actually the Commandment read: "No animal shall drink alcohol TO EXCESS（过量）."
